questions.q: Who sets the minimum age at which a child may shoot?

options.text: National law and the ground's rules
The parents alone, as they wish
The company that made the gun

questions.explain: The age depends on the country's law, the club's rules and its insurance, so check them first.

questions.q: What gun is a child often given in the first sessions?

options.text: A heavy 12 gauge with long barrels
A light 20 gauge with soft cartridges
Any gun the family has at home

questions.explain: A 20 gauge suits a smaller body and is fired with light cartridges; it is the light cartridge, not the light gun, that makes the recoil softer.

questions.q: How should a child's first session end?

options.text: With the hardest target of the day
When the box of cartridges is empty
On a good shot, before the child tires

questions.explain: Ending on a success leaves a good memory and the wish to come back.

questions.q: What does the FITASC Junior category tell a parent?

options.text: The youngest age to start shooting
The competition class for ages 13 to 20
The age at which a gun may be bought

questions.explain: Junior is a competition category (from 2027: from the year a shooter turns 13 to the year they turn 20); it says nothing about the age to start.

questions.q: A coach says 'Watch the next bird.' What will you see?

options.text: A live pigeon released from a box
A clay target thrown by a trap
A bird-shaped paper target on a board
A drone

questions.explain: 'Bird' is shooters' slang for a clay target; the FITASC rules forbid shooting at live animals.

questions.q: What does a shotgun fire?

options.text: One single bullet
A small arrow-like dart
A cloud of small pellets (shot)
A ball filled with paint

questions.explain: The shot leaves the muzzle as a small cloud of pellets, so the shooter points ahead of the moving target.

questions.q: Which statement about Compak® Sporting is correct?

options.text: A compact version on one field, stations in a line
It is a course of stands spread through a forest
It is shot only at live game birds in the field
It uses a single trap and a single station

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting brings Sporting™-style targets onto one small field with five stations and six traps.

questions.q: What do you shoot at in clay shooting?

options.text: Live birds released from a box
Clay targets thrown by a trap
Paper targets fixed on a board

questions.explain: You shoot only at artificial targets thrown by a trap. Shooting at live animals is forbidden.

questions.q: What is a trap?

options.text: A shotgun with a short barrel
The referee who runs the stand
A machine that throws targets

questions.explain: A trap is the machine that throws a target into the air or rolls it along the ground.

questions.q: Why does a shooter point the gun ahead of a moving target?

options.text: The shot needs time to reach the target
The referee asks all shooters to do it
It keeps the gun from touching the target

questions.explain: The target moves and the shot takes time to get there, so the gun points where the target will be a moment later.

questions.q: Which first step does this lesson suggest?

options.text: Buy a gun and practise alone
A taster lesson with a coach
Watch videos, then enter a championship

questions.explain: A coach teaches safety and good basics from the very start.

questions.q: Does a beginner need their own gun?

options.text: Yes, grounds do not lend guns
Yes, and it must be a pump-action
No, many grounds hire guns out

questions.explain: Many grounds have club guns you can shoot under supervision; the rules depend on national law.

questions.q: Which gun is NOT allowed in FITASC competitions?

options.text: A pump-action gun
A 12-gauge over-and-under
A semi-automatic

questions.explain: Pump-action guns are not allowed. A semi-automatic is allowed, but it may be loaded with two cartridges at most.

questions.q: Where do you find the exact rules for under-age shooters?

options.text: In local law and the club's rules
On any shooting forum online
Nowhere: they are the same worldwide

questions.explain: Rules differ between countries, so the sources are local law, the club and the federation.

questions.q: What is a federation sports licence?

options.text: A permit to buy and keep a gun
Proof of membership for its events
A referee's card for competitions

questions.explain: A sports licence is about entering competitions, not about the right to own a gun.

questions.q: What does a club usually ask for when a child joins?

options.text: Nothing: children just come along
The child's own registered gun
Written consent from the parents

questions.explain: Parental consent is a usual club requirement; sometimes insurance and a medical certificate are added.

questions.q: Which of these is a regular cost?

options.text: Your own gun
Cartridges and targets
A gun safe

questions.explain: Cartridges and targets are used up at each session.

questions.q: How many cartridges should you take for a round of 25 targets?

options.text: At least 25, plus spares
10, the ground adds more
Exactly 25, no spares

questions.explain: You need one cartridge per target, and you may fire a second shot at a single target, so take spares.

questions.q: How does a beginner usually start?

options.text: Buys an expensive gun first
Enters a championship abroad
A taster session with a coach

questions.explain: A taster session with a hired gun lets you try the sport without big spending.

questions.q: When do you usually need a European Firearms Pass?

options.text: For a lesson at your local ground
When you hire a gun abroad
Taking your own gun across the EU

questions.explain: The pass is issued by the EU country where you live, for travelling with your own guns. Without it, you can hire a gun at the destination.

questions.q: Where may you load the gun?

options.text: Anywhere at the ground, if the gun points at the ground
Only on the stand, pointing down the range, once shooting is allowed
On the way to the stand, so you are ready when called

questions.explain: Cartridges go in only on the stand, with the gun pointing down the range, after the referee or instructor allows shooting.

questions.q: What must you do before turning round on the stand?

options.text: Open the gun and take out all cartridges, fired or not
Put the safety catch on and keep the gun closed
Take out only the unfired cartridges, then close the gun

questions.explain: You turn round only with the gun open and empty; a safety catch is no substitute for an open gun.

questions.q: The gun clicks but does not fire. What should the shooter do?

options.text: Open it at once to see what went wrong
Turn round and show the gun to the coach
Stay put, gun down the range, and wait for the referee
Put the safety on and call for the target again

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require the shooter to stay put until the referee inspects; opening or touching the safety first scores zero.

questions.q: How many cartridges may a semi-automatic hold?

options.text: One only
As many as the magazine takes
No more than two

questions.explain: In both disciplines a semi-automatic may hold no more than two cartridges.

questions.q: How is a semi-automatic carried between stands?

options.text: Closed, with the safety catch on
With the action open, muzzle up or down
On a sling over the shoulder, unloaded
With one cartridge in, safety on

questions.explain: Guns are carried open, semi-automatics with the action open, muzzles straight up or down; slings are not allowed.

questions.q: Someone shouts “Cease fire!”. What is the interpreter’s first job?

options.text: Repeat “Stop!” loudly and check that the guns are open
Explain to the guests why shooting has stopped
Ask the coach quietly what has happened
Wait until a guest asks what is going on

questions.explain: An emergency stop is repeated at once; explanations come only when all guns are open.

questions.q: Lightning is close and the referee has paused shooting. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the gun closed and wait on the stand
Open and unload the gun, then shelter in a building
Shelter under the nearest tall tree with your gun

questions.explain: During any pause the gun is open and empty, and in lightning you leave the open ground for a building.

questions.q: Where should the coach be while a child is shooting in a training session?

options.text: Behind the squad, where he can watch the whole stand
Right beside the child, able to take the gun at once
At the trap, ready to stop the targets

questions.explain: In training, direct supervision means the coach stands next to the child and can step in at once. In a competition the referee runs the stand.

questions.q: Your daughter only comes to watch a competition. Does she need hearing protection?

options.text: Yes, the rules require it near the layout
No, only the people who are shooting need it
Only if she stands right next to the stand

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require hearing protection for spectators near the layout; in Sporting™ children outside the clubhouse wear it at all times.

questions.q: What should you do when a child gets tired during a session?

options.text: Add one more round to build character
Switch to a harder target to keep interest
Stop the session: tiredness lowers attention

questions.explain: When attention drops the risk of a gun-handling mistake rises, so it is better to stop.

questions.q: How are guns and cartridges usually stored at home?

options.text: In the gun slip under the bed, ready for training
In a cupboard the child can open, but unloaded
In a locked safe, cartridges apart, keys with adults

questions.explain: Store guns as the law of your country requires; usually a locked safe, cartridges separately, keys only with adults.

questions.q: Who must wear hearing protection at a competition?

options.text: Only the shooter who is on the stand
Shooters and referees, but not spectators
Everyone near the layout, spectators too

questions.explain: The rules of both disciplines name shooters, referees, staff and spectators near the layout.

questions.q: Your shooter walks onto the stand without safety glasses. How do the rules treat him?

options.text: He gets a warning and may shoot
He may shoot if the coach agrees
He loses one target
He is treated as absent

questions.explain: In both disciplines a shooter without eye or ear protection on the stand is treated as absent and may not shoot.

questions.q: Which gives the most hearing protection when many shots are fired?

options.text: Earplugs and ear muffs worn together
Electronic muffs with the volume turned up
Earplugs pushed in loosely, for comfort

questions.explain: Plugs and muffs together protect most, as long as both fit well.

questions.q: What is the advantage of electronic ear muffs?

options.text: They make safety glasses unnecessary
They soften the shot but let voices through
They block all sound, voices included

questions.explain: You are protected from the bang and still hear the referee’s commands.

questions.q: Which shorts are allowed at a FITASC competition?

options.text: Any sports shorts, as long as the shirt has sleeves
Bermuda-style shorts, ending no more than 5 cm above the knee
Short shorts in Compak® Sporting, but not in Sporting™
No shorts of any length, in either discipline

questions.explain: Short shorts are banned in both disciplines; long Bermuda-style shorts are accepted.

questions.q: Why are electronic ear muffs a good choice for an interpreter?

options.text: They soften the shot but let voices through
They are not required for interpreters
They block all sound completely
They record the coach

questions.explain: Hearing protection is compulsory near a layout, and electronic muffs let you hear the coach and referee.

questions.q: At an outdoor ground, how does much of the lead reach a shooter?

options.text: Through the skin of the face, from the smoke of each shot
Mainly from drinking tap water at the ground
Through the hands, from cartridges and cases to the mouth

questions.explain: Lead dust moves from cartridges, cases and the gun to the hands, and from the hands to food and the mouth.

questions.q: Where is a good place for a snack at the ground?

options.text: Right on the stand, between your turns
In the clubhouse, after washing your hands
While you pick up your empty cases

questions.explain: Eat away from the stand and only with clean hands.

questions.q: How can you check your lead exposure?

options.text: With a blood test arranged by a doctor
From the colour of your fingernails
It cannot be measured at all

questions.explain: A blood test shows how much lead is in your blood, mostly from recent exposure; talk to a doctor about it.

questions.q: What is a good habit with the clothes you shot in?

options.text: Wear them at home for the rest of the day
Shake them out in the car and wear them again
Change, and wash them apart from children’s things

questions.explain: Shooting clothes carry lead dust, so change after shooting and wash them separately.

questions.q: What happens when a child shoots a gun that is too long?

options.text: They lean back and feel more recoil
Nothing changes; it is even easier
The targets seem to fly more slowly
The pattern becomes much denser

questions.explain: A gun that is too long spoils the stance, makes recoil worse and can frighten the child.

questions.q: What is the length of pull?

options.text: The length of the barrels to the muzzle
From the trigger to the middle of the butt pad
The weight of the gun with its chokes
From the rib down to the top of the comb

questions.explain: This is the measure most often changed to make a gun fit a child.

questions.q: When is it worth buying a child their own gun?

options.text: Before the very first session at a ground
Only a brand-new and very expensive model
Once interest is steady, with a coach's advice
As soon as the child can lift an adult gun

questions.explain: Hire and second-hand models first; buy once it is clear the child will carry on.

questions.q: Why do many shooters begin with a coach rather than teach themselves?

options.text: Lessons with a coach cost less than shooting alone
A coach watches safety and catches faults before they set in
The rules do not allow shooting without a coach nearby

questions.explain: Faults are hard to feel from behind the gun, and a habit that has set in takes longer to change than to learn well from the start.

questions.q: What does a coach usually check at the first lesson?

options.text: Your ranking in national competitions
How many cartridges you can carry
Which of your eyes is the master eye

questions.explain: The master eye decides whether the gun points where you look. If your master eye is on the other side from the shoulder you shoot from (for example, left eye, right shoulder), the coach suggests a fix. Common fixes are closing one eye or putting a dot on your glasses.

questions.q: A trial lesson felt unclear and uncomfortable. What do many shooters do next?

options.text: Try a lesson with another coach
Give up clay shooting for good
Put up with it and change nothing

questions.explain: Coaches explain in different ways, and looking for one who suits you is normal.

questions.q: Who should explain shooting technique to the child?

options.text: The coach, in training
Any experienced shooter nearby
The parents, during each shot

questions.explain: One voice, the coach's, does not confuse the child; the parents support.

questions.q: Which goal is a process goal?

options.text: Win the whole competition
My routine on each target
Break 25 out of 25 targets

questions.explain: A process goal is about what the child controls, not about the final score.

questions.q: May a parent give tips from behind the stand during a competition?

options.text: Yes, if they speak quietly
Yes, between two targets
No, it counts as coaching

questions.explain: Coaching during a competition can earn the child a yellow card, and the person coaching is sent away.

questions.q: What can a parent do right after a bad round?

options.text: Explain all the mistakes at once, in detail
Let the child start the talk later
Compare the score with the other children

questions.explain: Give the child time to cool down; going over the round is the coach's job when the child is ready.

questions.q: Does a spectator need hearing protection?

options.text: No, only the people who are shooting
Yes, the rules require it near the layout
Only at championships, not at club shoots

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require hearing protection for shooters, referees, staff and spectators near the layout.

questions.q: May you take photos with flash?

options.text: Yes, if you stay in the spectator area
Only once the referee has agreed
No, because flash can dazzle the shooter

questions.explain: Flash distracts and dazzles the shooter, so spectators do not use it.

questions.q: What happens if a spectator coaches a shooter during a competition?

options.text: The shooter can get a yellow card; the adviser is sent away
Nothing at all, as long as the advice is given quietly
The shooter must shoot the whole stand again from the start

questions.explain: Advice during a competition counts as coaching, which both rulebooks forbid.

questions.q: When is it right to applaud?

options.text: While the shooter is aiming at the target
After the stand, when nobody is about to call
Just before the shooter calls “pull”

questions.explain: While anyone on the layout is shooting or about to call, spectators stay quiet; applause comes when the shooter has finished.

questions.q: Where may a spectator stand?

options.text: In front of the firing line, for a better view
Next to the traps, out of the line of fire
In the spectator area, behind the stand

questions.explain: Spectators stand in the area set aside for them, usually behind the stand.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, a spectator loudly criticises a ruling. How do the rules see this?

options.text: As an attempt to influence the referee
As normal support from the crowd
As a breach of the dress code

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting the rules count open criticism of a decision by shooters or spectators, without the referee’s permission, as an attempt to influence.

questions.q: What do you need to film a competition with a drone?

options.text: Nothing, as long as it flies above the stands
The organiser’s permission, plus the country’s drone rules
Permission from one of the shooters in the squad

questions.explain: Flying over a shooting ground needs the organiser’s permission, and the drone rules of the country always apply.

questions.q: What happens if you come to the stand without hearing protection or safety glasses?

options.text: You may shoot, but you get a warning
You are treated as absent and may not shoot
The referee gives you a spare set

questions.explain: In both disciplines a shooter without hearing protection or safety glasses is treated as absent, and the lateness rules apply.

questions.q: Where may you check that your gun works?

options.text: On the first competition stand, before the round
Anywhere on the ground, if the area is clear
At a special test stand, if the ground has one

questions.explain: Test shots on a competition stand are not allowed in either discipline; use the test stand.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting shot by squad, a shooter arrives after the first shooter has called for the first target. What happens?

options.text: Nothing, he joins in
He gets 25 zeros for that round
He shoots the round alone later without penalty
He loses one target

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting shot by squad, arriving after the first call costs 25 zeros for the round. For a reason outside your control, you can appeal to the jury in writing on the same day.

questions.q: What is the largest number of shooters in a squad?
questions.explain: In both Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting a squad has at most 6 shooters.

questions.q: Two shooters tie for 5th place. How are they ranked?

options.text: By a 25-target shoot-off for that place
By drawing lots after the event has ended
They share it; countback from the 8th layout or Compak sets the order
By age, with the younger shooter placed higher

questions.explain: Shoot-offs are only for the top three. Below that, tied shooters share the place, and countback compares the 8th layout or Compak, then the 7th, and so on.

questions.q: In Compak in line, when do you count as late?

options.text: When your number is cancelled in the system and the next shooter is on station 1
As soon as the referee has called out your name for the first time
Only after the whole group has finished shooting the round

questions.explain: Both things must have happened: your number is already cancelled in the computer system, and the next shooter stands on station 1. The penalty is 25 zeros for the round.

questions.q: How do you carry your gun between stands?

options.text: Open, so everyone can see it is not loaded, and without a sling
Closed and unloaded, on a sling over your shoulder
Closed, with the safety catch on, pointing at the ground

questions.explain: Guns are carried open and slings are not allowed; a semi-automatic is carried with its breech open.

questions.q: Who is in the Junior category in the FITASC table from 2027?

options.text: Everyone up to the year they turn 25
From the year they turn 13 to the year they turn 20
Only boys, from the year they turn 12 to 16

questions.explain: Junior runs from 1 January of the year a shooter turns 13 to 31 December of the year they turn 20, for girls and boys.

questions.q: Does a junior take part in the open ranking?

options.text: No, only in the Junior ranking
Only if they win the Junior ranking
Yes, together with the Junior ranking

questions.explain: One score counts in both the open ranking and the category ranking.

questions.q: What is usually the largest regular cost?

options.text: Targets and cartridges
Medals and trophies
A new gun each season

questions.explain: Targets and cartridges are used at each session, so budget for them first.

questions.q: A parent calls out advice to their child during the round. What can happen?

options.text: Nothing; parents may give advice
A yellow card, and the parent is sent away
The whole round is shot again

questions.explain: Coaching during the competition is not allowed: the shooter gets a yellow card and the person coaching is sent out of the shooting area.
